samples.summary: §6 interpolates scorer-supplied strings (including finding keys taken verbatim from CodeRabbit comment text) into the committed markdown report with no escaping
samples.evidence: `renderValidity` writes the scorer payload's own strings straight into the document: `for (const reason of v.completeness.reasons) out.push(`- ${reason}`)` (report.mjs, new §6 render block), plus table rows built from `g.arm`/`g.axis`/`g.bucket` and `x.what_would_change_it`. Those reasons are produced by `validity.mjs` and embed attacker-influenceable text: `scripts/agent/eval/validity.mjs:897` pushes `join.unmatched_keys.slice(0,5).map((u) => u.finding_key).join(" · ")`, and a `finding_key` is `${file}::${summary.toLowerCase()}` where `summary` is carried VERBATIM off a CodeRabbit review comment (`scripts/agent/eval/adapters/coderabbit.test.mjs:869-877`). CodeRabbit's comment text is influenced by whoever opens a pull request in the repo under review, so a crafted file name or claim wording containing `|`, backticks or a newline is echoed unescaped into a report that the eval-score lane prints to the job log and commits to `dlgpdmsly2/wafflebase-agent-eval` (.github/workflows/eval-score.yml:210-236). Effect is content spoofing of a benchmark document (forged table rows / fabricated figures), not code execution. I could not confirm that a summary can carry a raw newline through the parser, hence low confidence. No escaping helper exists anywhere in report.mjs (grepped for escape/sanitiz).

samples.summary: Rendering the validity scorer's completeness reasons puts absolute local filesystem paths into a report committed to the eval store repository
samples.evidence: The new §6 block prints every `completeness.reasons` entry verbatim (`out.push(`- ${reason}`)`). `scripts/agent/eval/validity.mjs:983` builds one of those reasons as `... could not be read ...: ${unreadableList.map((u) => u.path).slice(0,5).join(" · ")}`, and the label reader records an ABSOLUTE path for an unreadable label (`scripts/agent/eval/adjudicate.test.mjs:466` asserts `read.unreadable[0].path === abs`). Before this change those paths only reached the scorer's own stderr; now they are baked into `reports/<comparison>.md`, which .github/workflows/eval-score.yml:210-236 cats into the job log and `git add`s into the store repo's permanent history. On a laptop run this discloses the operator's home directory / username; in CI it discloses runner paths. Low-impact information disclosure in a permanent artifact.

samples.summary: reviewerFigures prints a config snapshot's identity fields without ever checking the snapshot's own config_hash against the report's pooling key
samples.evidence: `reviewerFigures` reads `config_id`, `target`, `sdk_version`, `config_hash_version` and `lenses[]` off `r.configSnapshot` and renders them as 'The reviewer these figures describe', but nothing compares `configSnapshot.config_hash` to the `--config-hash` the report is filed under. The only cross-check in the render path is `report.mjs:2971`, which compares `run.runJson.config_hash` and is skipped entirely when that field is falsy (`if (run.runJson?.config_hash && ...)`). `store.getRun` (store.mjs:848-873) performs no hash validation on read; `putRun` only compares a NEW snapshot against a stored one (store.mjs:816-841). So a run whose `run.json` omits `config_hash` — a hand-written or older envelope — lets the human-readable reviewer block describe lenses/models belonging to a different configuration than the `config_hash` printed one table above it, which is the pooling key readers are told to trust. Low confidence because the runner always writes `config_hash` into run.json (run.mjs:830-839), so this needs a hand-edited or legacy envelope.

samples.summary: The driver's refuse-on-non-zero-exit gate is relaxed for validity, and the only confirmation of the tolerated exit is the same failing process's self-reported verdict
samples.evidence: `if (r.status !== 0 && r.status !== tolerated) refuse(...)` (score-all.mjs:722) now accepts exit 1 from `validity.mjs`, and `assertPartialIsDeclared` (score-all.mjs:~447) validates that exit only against `payload.completeness.verdict === "partial"` — a field emitted by the very process whose exit code is in doubt. Any failure mode in which validity emits a partial-verdict JSON and exits 1 (e.g. a CodeRabbit arm that came back empty for a credential/scope reason rather than an absent-labels reason) is filed as a legitimate score and committed, which is the outcome the preflight and DEGRADATION_MARKERS exist to prevent. Mitigating: `assertNoDegradation(r.stderr, ...)` still runs on validity's stderr and the adapter's endpoint-absent markers (score-all.mjs:126-137) would fire for the common API-failure shapes, so I could not complete an exploit chain — hence low confidence. Flagged because it is a guard being loosened on the path that files data others trust.
